Where it began

Ravichandran Ashwin was born in Madras, the city later renamed Chennai, on 17 September 1986, and began playing at nine for YMCA. He started out as an opening batter, good enough to open for India's Under-17 side, and tried medium pace before a coach steered him towards off-spin. It proved to be quite a suggestion.

Tamil Nadu gave him his first-class start in 2006, and he took six Haryana wickets on debut, and was soon captaining the side. With Chennai Super Kings he won the IPL in 2010 and 2011, and was named player of the 2010 Champions League Twenty20.

The player

His Test career began against West Indies at Delhi in November 2011, with his cap handed to him by Sachin Tendulkar. He took 6 for 47 in the second innings and was man of the match. In only his third Test he made his first hundred as well as taking five wickets.

Between 2011 and 2024 he played 106 Tests, taking 537 wickets at 24.01, with 37 five-wicket innings and 8 ten-wicket matches, and a best of 7 for 59 against New Zealand in 2016. He also made 3,503 runs at 25.76, with six hundreds. In 2013 he took 29 wickets as India beat Australia 4–0, and in 2016 he took 82 wickets in a home season. That year the ICC named him its Cricketer of the Year and its Test Cricketer of the Year. He was also part of the sides that won the 2011 World Cup and the 2013 Champions Trophy.

What made him special

His great gift was thought. Coaches noticed early how he used the angles and the width of the crease and seemed to know what a batter was about to try. To his off-breaks he added an arm ball and a carrom ball, the latter grown out of a flicked delivery from tennis-ball games in the streets of Chennai. Four times he managed the rare double of a hundred and five wickets in one Test.

Overseas pitches were a sterner examination than the turning tracks at home, and abroad the wickets tended to come a little more slowly. The batters of India, at least, never had to face him.

Away from the middle

He played county cricket for Worcestershire and Nottinghamshire, and led Dindigul Dragons to the Tamil Nadu Premier League title in 2024. He took to YouTube, analysing matches and reviewing films, and he mentored young players at his own academy in Chennai. In 2024 he published a memoir, I Have the Streets, written with Sidharth Monga. India gave him the Arjuna award in 2015 and the Padma Shri in 2025, and in March 2025 a street in West Mambalam, the part of Chennai where he lived, was approved to be renamed Ravichandran Ashwin Street.

And finally

Eleven times he was named player of a Test series, a tally that, by November 2026, only Muttiah Muralitharan had matched. Not bad for a boy who was only turned into a spinner because his batting needed a little help.
